title: Legacy Modernisation Strategies
objectives: Plan and execute legacy system modernisation with pragmatism and rigour
Apply the CDDO Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework to prioritise modernisation
Choose between modernisation strategies: strangler fig, rebuild, replatform, wrap and extend
Build business cases for legacy modernisation that survive Treasury scrutiny
Manage the political, commercial, and human dimensions of legacy transformation
whyThisMatters:
Legacy technology is the defining challenge of UK government technology. The State of Digital Government Review identified outdated IT systems and ageing data as a key source of inefficiency and a major constraint to modernising government services. The National Audit Office has repeatedly flagged the cost of legacy, estimating billions in accumulated debt across departments.

This is not an abstract problem. Legacy systems process benefit payments for millions of citizens, manage tax collection, run border systems, and support the criminal justice system. When they fail, real people are affected — incorrect payments, processing delays, security vulnerabilities. When they cannot be changed, policy ambitions are blocked — new services cannot be built, data cannot be shared, and digital transformation stalls.

The CDDO Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework provides a standard mechanism for gauging the technical health of legacy IT assets across government. It enables strategic allocation of focus and funding. But the framework only identifies the problem — it does not solve it. Solution architects are the people who design and deliver the modernisation strategies that actually move systems from legacy to sustainable.

content.heading: What Makes a System Legacy (And What Does Not)
content.body:
A system is not legacy because it is old. A system is legacy because it can no longer be changed safely, economically, or quickly enough to meet the organisation's needs. A ten-year-old system that is well-structured, well-tested, and easy to modify is not legacy. A two-year-old system built in a rush with no tests, no documentation, and tightly coupled to a specific vendor's obsolete API version is already legacy.

The CDDO Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework assesses systems across two dimensions: Likelihood (how likely are negative outcomes) scored from 1 to 6, and Impact (how severe would those outcomes be) scored from 1 to 5. Systems receive a combined risk score that places them in a risk matrix.

Factors that make a system legacy include: technology components that are no longer supported or patched (creating security vulnerability), a shrinking pool of people with the skills to maintain it (creating operational risk), architecture that prevents the system from integrating with modern services (creating capability constraint), absence of automated testing (making any change high-risk), absence of documentation (making knowledge dependent on individuals), contractual arrangements that make change prohibitively expensive (creating commercial lock-in), and data structures that cannot accommodate new requirements (creating policy constraint).

The framework is not just about identifying risk — it is about enabling strategic allocation. Not every legacy system needs immediate modernisation. Some are stable, low-risk, and can continue operating with minimal investment. Others are critical, high-risk, and require urgent intervention. The framework helps prioritise by showing where the intersection of high likelihood and high impact creates unacceptable risk.

As an architect, your role is to assess legacy systems honestly — neither downplaying risk (which defers necessary investment) nor exaggerating it (which creates false urgency and diverts resources from genuine priorities). The framework gives you a structured, defensible approach to this assessment.

content.heading: Modernisation Strategies: A Taxonomy
content.body:
There is no single approach to legacy modernisation. The right strategy depends on the system's risk profile, the organisation's constraints, the available budget, and the urgency of the need. Six strategies cover most situations.

Retain (also called 'wrap and manage'): Keep the legacy system running but invest in monitoring, documentation, and operational resilience. Appropriate when the system is stable, low-risk, and meeting current needs — or when the cost of replacement exceeds the cost of continued operation. This is a legitimate strategy, not a failure to modernise. Many government systems should be retained until there is a genuine trigger for change.

Wrap and Extend: Place a modern API layer or service layer around the legacy system, exposing its data and functions through modern interfaces while leaving the core unchanged. Appropriate when the system's data or logic is still valuable but its interfaces are outdated. This is the fastest route to enabling modern integration without the risk of changing the core system.

Replatform: Move the system to a modern infrastructure (typically cloud) without changing its architecture or code significantly. Lift-and-shift to virtual machines, containerisation of existing applications, or migration to managed database services. Appropriate when infrastructure obsolescence is the primary risk (end-of-support operating systems, ageing hardware) but the application logic is sound.

Refactor (also called 'strangler fig'): Gradually replace components of the legacy system with modern equivalents, routing traffic progressively from old to new. The legacy system is 'strangled' as more and more of its functionality moves to the new architecture. Appropriate for large, complex systems where a big-bang replacement is too risky. Named after the strangler fig tree that grows around its host until the host dies.

Rebuild: Build a completely new system to replace the legacy one, then migrate users and data in a planned cutover. Appropriate when the legacy system's architecture, data model, and business logic are all fundamentally unsuitable and incremental improvement is not viable. Highest risk and cost, but sometimes the only option.

Retire: Decommission the system entirely, migrating its essential data elsewhere and redirecting users to alternative services. Appropriate when the system's function is no longer needed, when it has been superseded by another service, or when its user base has shrunk below the threshold where maintenance is justified.

content.heading: Choosing the Right Strategy
content.body:
The choice between strategies is not purely technical. It involves cost, risk, capability, and politics. Several factors guide the decision.

Urgency of the trigger: If the primary driver is an end-of-support deadline (a platform reaching end-of-life in 12 months), replatforming may be the only feasible response in the available time. If the driver is a new capability requirement that the legacy system cannot support, wrapping or refactoring may be faster than rebuilding.

System complexity: Simple systems with well-understood logic can be rebuilt relatively safely. Complex systems with decades of accumulated business rules, edge cases, and undocumented behaviours are dangerous to rebuild because knowledge inevitably gets lost. For complex systems, the strangler fig approach is often safer because it preserves existing behaviour by default, replacing components one at a time with verified equivalence.

Data sensitivity: Systems handling sensitive data (personal data, financial data, security-classified information) require modernisation approaches that maintain data integrity and security throughout the transition. Parallel running (operating old and new systems simultaneously with data synchronisation) is common but expensive and complex.

Skills availability: Modernisation requires skills in both the legacy technology (to understand what exists) and the target technology (to build the replacement). If legacy skills are scarce (COBOL, specific proprietary platforms), the window for modernisation is closing — the longer you wait, the harder it becomes to find people who understand what needs to be replaced.

Commercial constraints: If the legacy system is operated under a long-term contract, the commercial terms may constrain modernisation options. Exit costs, intellectual property ownership, data extraction rights, and transition obligations all shape what is practically achievable.

Appetite for risk: Rebuilds are higher risk than incremental approaches. If the system is critical (processing payments, managing security, supporting essential services), the organisation's risk appetite will likely push toward lower-risk strategies even if they are slower or more expensive.

A useful heuristic: start with the least disruptive strategy that addresses the actual problem. If the problem is infrastructure end-of-support, replatform. If the problem is integration capability, wrap. If the problem is fundamental architectural constraint, refactor. Only rebuild if nothing less will work — and even then, consider whether a phased rebuild (strangler fig) is possible before committing to big-bang replacement.

content.heading: The Strangler Fig Pattern in Government
content.body:
The strangler fig pattern deserves special attention because it is the most commonly appropriate strategy for large government legacy systems. These systems are typically too large and too critical for big-bang replacement, but too constrained for mere wrapping to solve.

The pattern works as follows: identify a bounded slice of functionality in the legacy system. Build a modern replacement for that slice. Route traffic for that functionality from the legacy system to the new component. Verify the new component works correctly. Repeat for the next slice. Eventually, the legacy system has no remaining traffic and can be decommissioned.

In government, the slicing strategy is crucial. Good slices are: a specific user journey (e.g., 'apply for a new licence' moved to a new service while 'renew existing licence' remains on legacy), a specific integration point (e.g., the API that external partners use is replaced with a modern API that routes to legacy internally), or a specific data domain (e.g., reference data management is extracted to a new service while transactional processing remains on legacy).

The routing mechanism is the architectural challenge. Options include: an API gateway that routes requests based on path or header to either legacy or new services, a message broker that distributes events to both systems during transition, or a reverse proxy that sends specific URL patterns to the new service while passing everything else to legacy.

Critical success factors in government strangler fig programmes include:

Verifiable equivalence: for each migrated slice, you must demonstrate that the new component produces the same outcomes as the legacy one. For systems that make financial calculations or determine eligibility, this requires parallel running or shadow testing where both systems process the same inputs and outputs are compared.

Rollback capability: if the new component fails or produces incorrect results, you must be able to route traffic back to legacy instantly. Design your routing mechanism to support instant rollback without data loss.

Data consistency: during transition, data may be modified in both legacy and new systems. You need a strategy for keeping them consistent — typically event-driven synchronisation or a shared data layer.

Incremental funding: the strangler fig approach suits government funding cycles because each slice can be funded independently. You do not need to secure the entire programme budget upfront — you can demonstrate value from early slices to justify continued investment.

content.heading: The Human and Political Dimensions
content.body:
Legacy modernisation is as much a human and political challenge as a technical one. Technical strategies that ignore these dimensions fail even when they are architecturally sound.

The knowledge problem: legacy systems accumulate decades of business knowledge, much of it undocumented and existing only in the heads of long-serving staff. When HMRC modernises a tax calculation system, the business rules are not just in code — they are in the interpretations, workarounds, and edge-case handling that experienced operators apply daily. Modernisation projects that do not invest heavily in knowledge extraction will produce systems that handle the standard cases correctly but fail on the edge cases that matter most.

The identity problem: staff who have maintained a legacy system for years often derive professional identity from their expertise. Modernisation can feel like a judgement on their work — 'the system they built is not good enough.' Engage these people as essential contributors to modernisation, not as obstacles to it. Their knowledge is irreplaceable and their buy-in determines whether the transition succeeds.

The vendor problem: many government legacy systems are maintained under long-term contracts with suppliers who have strong commercial incentives to resist modernisation. Their revenue depends on continued maintenance of the existing system. They may claim ownership of key intellectual property, charge prohibitive exit fees, or provide minimal support for data extraction. The Sourcing Playbook addresses this — building clear exit provisions into contracts from the start. But for existing contracts, the architect must work within commercial constraints.

The political problem: legacy modernisation is invisible work. It does not produce new services that citizens see or ministers can announce. It competes for funding against visible new capabilities. Building the political case requires connecting modernisation to outcomes that leaders care about: 'we cannot deliver the Minister's priority without modernising this platform' is more compelling than 'this system is technically outdated.' The Digital Assurance Playbook explicitly checks whether initiatives tackle existing legacy debt — this gives architects a policy hook for justifying investment.

The fear problem: large modernisation programmes in government have a poor track record. Decision-makers remember failures — programmes that went over budget, over time, or delivered systems that did not work. This creates institutional caution. Address it by proposing incremental approaches with clear off-ramps: if phase 1 fails, we have spent £X and learned Y, rather than committing £50 million upfront with no exit points.

content.heading: Preventing Future Legacy
content.body:
Modernisation addresses the legacy you have inherited. Prevention addresses the legacy you might create. The best modernisation strategy is not needing one — designing systems today that will not become legacy tomorrow.

The government's guidance on preventing technical debt and legacy sets clear expectations. All legacy technology associated with a product or service must be scored against the Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework. But prevention goes beyond scoring.

Architectural decisions that prevent future legacy include:

Using supported, actively maintained technology with a clear roadmap. Choose platforms, frameworks, and languages with large communities, active development, and predictable long-term support. Avoid niche technologies where the risk of abandonment is high.

Designing for replaceability. Every component should be replaceable independently. This means well-defined interfaces (APIs between components), minimal coupling (changes to one component do not cascade), and clear separation of concerns. If you can replace the database layer without rewriting the application layer, you have designed for replaceability.

Using evergreen, always-updated services where possible. Managed cloud services that are automatically updated by the provider eliminate the end-of-support problem for those components. The trade-off is reduced control — but for most government services, the benefits of automatic patching and version management outweigh the cost of reduced control.

Maintaining documentation as a living practice. Systems become legacy partly because knowledge is lost when people leave. Automated architecture documentation (generated from code), maintained ADRs, and operational runbooks reduce the knowledge loss that makes systems unmaintainable.

Investing in automated testing. Systems without tests cannot be changed safely. They become legacy by definition because every modification is high-risk. Building comprehensive automated tests from the start — and maintaining them as the system evolves — is the single most important investment in preventing future legacy.

Building in commercial flexibility. Contracts should include clear exit provisions, data extraction rights, and technology transfer obligations. The Sourcing Playbook and Commercial Playbooks provide guidance on preventing commercial lock-in that creates technical legacy.

content.heading: Measuring Modernisation Progress
content.body:
Legacy modernisation programmes can run for years. Without clear metrics, they risk becoming perpetual programmes that consume budget without demonstrating progress.

Technical health metrics measure the condition of the system being modernised. The Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework provides a starting score. As modernisation progresses, rescore the system at defined intervals. A dropping risk score is the clearest indicator of progress. Specific technical metrics include: percentage of components on supported versions, automated test coverage, mean time to deploy changes, mean time to recover from failure, and number of security vulnerabilities in the backlog.

Delivery velocity metrics measure whether modernisation is making the system easier to change. Track the time and cost of delivering new features or policy changes. If modernisation is working, feature delivery should become faster and cheaper over time. If it is not, something has gone wrong — you may be modernising the wrong components, or the new architecture is introducing its own complexity.

Risk reduction metrics measure whether the most critical risks are being addressed. If the primary risk was skills availability (only three people can maintain the system), track how many people can now work on the modernised components. If the primary risk was security (unpatched vulnerabilities), track the vulnerability count over time.

Business outcome metrics connect modernisation to organisational objectives. Can the system now support policy changes it previously could not? Has service availability improved? Has the cost of operation reduced? These are the metrics that justify continued investment to programme boards.

Report metrics at appropriate cadences: weekly to the delivery team, monthly to the programme board, quarterly to the investment committee. At each level, translate the metrics into the audience's language — the delivery team cares about test coverage; the investment committee cares about whether their money is producing measurable improvement.

A warning sign: if modernisation metrics show the system getting healthier but delivery velocity is not improving, you may be modernising infrastructure without addressing the architectural constraints that actually slow delivery. Replatforming a monolith does not make it less monolithic — it just moves the same constraints to a new environment.

workedExample.title: Strangler Fig Modernisation of a DESNZ Licensing System
workedExample.context: DESNZ operates a licensing system that manages 45,000 active energy installation licences. Built in 2008 on a .NET Framework 4.5 application with a SQL Server monolithic database, the system handles licence applications, renewals, variations, compliance checks, and enforcement actions. The application server runs on Windows Server 2016 (approaching extended end-of-support), the .NET Framework version is no longer receiving feature updates, and the database has grown to 3TB with no archiving strategy. Three contractors understand the codebase. The system processes £12 million in licence fees annually and cannot be taken offline. Policy teams need four new licence types introduced within 18 months to comply with new legislation. The current system cannot accommodate new licence types without 6 months of development per type due to tightly coupled business rules.
workedExample.approach:
The Solution Architect proposes a strangler fig approach, prioritising the new licence types as the first slice.

Phase 1 (months 1-6): New Licence Types on Modern Platform
Build a new microservice for the four new licence types on a cloud-native platform (.NET 8 on containers, PostgreSQL). Route all applications for new licence types to the new service. The legacy system continues handling all existing 45,000 licences unchanged. An API gateway routes based on licence type. Data synchronisation keeps a read-only copy of new licences in the legacy database for reporting.

Result: New legislation requirement met without touching the legacy system. Policy teams have their four new licence types. Risk to existing operations: zero.

Phase 2 (months 7-12): Extract Renewals
The renewal journey (40% of all transactions) is extracted to the new platform. A renewal microservice handles the workflow, integrating with GOV.UK Pay for fee collection and GOV.UK Notify for communications. The legacy system's renewal function is disabled for licence types migrated, with the API gateway routing renewal requests to the appropriate system based on licence type.

Result: 40% of transaction volume moved to modern platform. Legacy system load reduces. Modern renewals complete in 3 working days versus 10 on legacy.

Phase 3 (months 13-18): Extract Compliance and Enforcement
Compliance checking and enforcement actions are extracted. This is the most complex slice due to integration with external data sources and complex business rules. The architect conducts a knowledge extraction programme with the three contractors to document all business rules before they leave.

Phase 4 (months 19-24): Migrate Remaining Licences and Decommission
Existing licences are migrated to the new platform in batches. Once all licences are migrated and verified, the legacy system is decommissioned. Data is archived per retention policy.

The architect's routing architecture uses an API gateway that makes the strangling invisible to users. From their perspective, they interact with a single licensing service — they do not know (and should not care) which backend handles their request.
workedExample.outcome: After 12 months, 60% of transactions are on the modern platform. Feature delivery time for the new licence types is 4 weeks per type (versus 6 months on legacy). The Legacy IT Risk Assessment score drops from 4/5 (high likelihood, high impact) to 2/3 (low likelihood, medium impact). The three contractors' knowledge has been documented and the new platform is maintained by a team of five civil servants. The programme secures continued funding for phases 3 and 4 based on demonstrated progress.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: Starting with the new licence types was strategically brilliant because it delivered visible policy value immediately without touching the legacy system. This built confidence with programme boards and justified continued investment. The phased approach meant each phase could be funded independently, avoiding the need for a large upfront commitment that might have been rejected. The knowledge extraction in phase 3 was the highest-risk activity — starting it earlier (in parallel with phase 2) would have been wiser.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Unmaintainable Benefits Calculation Engine
civilServiceScenario.background: A government department processes means-tested benefits for 2.3 million claimants, disbursing £8.4 billion annually. The calculation engine is a 25-year-old COBOL system running on a mainframe. The vendor's contract expires in 14 months with no option to extend. Only two people in the UK can maintain the COBOL code, one of whom retires in 8 months. The system has no automated tests and no documentation beyond handwritten notes from 2004. The calculation rules are embedded in 180,000 lines of COBOL and include policy exceptions accumulated over two decades that no single person fully understands. A recent policy change required 4 months of development, manual regression testing, and still introduced a defect that caused 12,000 incorrect payments totalling £3.2 million. The department has secured £35 million over three years for modernisation but has not yet chosen a strategy.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You must recommend a modernisation strategy that is technically sound, financially viable within £35 million, and does not risk disrupting payments to 2.3 million claimants at any point during transition. The system cannot have unplanned downtime. Payments must be calculated correctly. The strategy must be deliverable within the contract expiry timeline.
constraints: 14 months until vendor contract expires — no extension possible
Only 2 people understand the COBOL code, one retiring in 8 months
180,000 lines of COBOL with no tests and no documentation
2.3 million claimants depend on correct, timely payments
£8.4 billion annually in payments — any calculation error is politically catastrophic
New policy changes are queued — the system must accommodate them during transition
No tolerance for payment disruption — even brief outages trigger parliamentary questions
The mainframe hosting contract can be extended separately from the development contract
The department has limited internal COBOL expertise
Parallel running of old and new calculation engines is possible but expensive to verify
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Lead Solution Architect responsible for recommending a modernisation strategy to the programme board. You must present options, a recommendation, and an honest assessment of risks.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This is one of the hardest scenarios in government technology. A full rebuild is tempting but carries extreme risk — reimplementing 25 years of calculation rules without documentation means inevitable errors, and errors mean incorrect payments to vulnerable people. The strangler fig approach is safer but 14 months is very tight for the first slice to be in production, especially when knowledge extraction is the prerequisite.

A pragmatic approach might be: immediately extend the mainframe hosting contract (separately from development) to buy more time. Commission an urgent knowledge extraction programme with the two remaining COBOL experts before one retires. Implement a parallel-running architecture where a new calculation engine runs alongside the COBOL engine, with outputs compared automatically for every calculation. Only route live payments through the new engine when parallel running demonstrates verified equivalence for each benefit type.

The key architecture decisions are: how to extract and codify the business rules (specification by example from the COBOL output), how to verify equivalence (parallel running with automated comparison), how to manage the transition (benefit type by benefit type, simplest first), and how to handle the rules that nobody fully understands (conservative approach: if the new engine disagrees with legacy, default to legacy until the discrepancy is investigated).

The £35 million budget is probably insufficient for a full replacement within 3 years given the complexity. Being honest about this is important — a phased approach that modernises the highest-risk benefit types first and extends to others in a subsequent funding period is more realistic than promising full replacement within budget.

practiceArtefact.description: Produce a two-page modernisation strategy paper for a departmental programme board. The subject is a 12-year-old case management system used by 800 caseworkers to manage 150,000 active cases. The system runs on an on-premise Java application server (end-of-support in 18 months), uses an Oracle database (licence renewal due in 6 months at £1.2 million per year), and has a web frontend built in a JavaScript framework that is no longer maintained. The system works but is slow (pages take 8-12 seconds to load), cannot support mobile working (caseworkers need to visit sites), and cannot integrate with a new department-wide document management system.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Structure your paper as: Problem Statement (why action is needed now), Options (at least 4 genuine strategies), Recommendation (with clear rationale), Risk Assessment (top 5 risks), and Next Steps. Keep it concise — programme boards do not read long documents. Use the Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework dimensions (Likelihood and Impact) to frame the urgency. Consider the commercial trigger (Oracle licence renewal) as a decision forcing function.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Legacy Modernisation Strategy: Case Management System**

For: Programme Board | Date: [Date] | Author: [Solution Architect]

**Problem Statement:**
Three converging triggers require action within 12 months: (1) Java application server reaches end-of-support in 18 months, creating security vulnerability; (2) Oracle database licence renewal in 6 months at £1.2M/year — renewing locks us into legacy for another 3 years; (3) inability to support mobile caseworkers or integrate with the new document management system blocks operational improvement. Legacy IT Risk Assessment: Likelihood 4, Impact 4 (high risk).

**Options:**

1. Retain and Replatform: Migrate the existing application to cloud containers, replace Oracle with PostgreSQL. Cost: £2.8M. Timeline: 12 months. Addresses infrastructure risk and Oracle cost, but retains the slow frontend and monolithic architecture.

2. Strangler Fig: Build new microservices for the highest-value workflows (case creation, site visits, document management integration) on a modern stack. Route these workflows to new services while legacy handles the remainder. Cost: £4.5M over 2 years. Timeline: first slice live in 6 months. Addresses all triggers progressively.

3. COTS Replacement: Procure a commercial case management platform and configure it. Cost: £3.2M implementation + £800K/year licensing. Timeline: 9 months to go-live. Addresses all triggers but creates vendor dependency and may not accommodate all 150,000 case types without expensive customisation.

4. Full Rebuild: Build a new cloud-native case management system from scratch. Cost: £6.2M over 18 months. Timeline: 18 months to full replacement. Highest risk and cost but produces the most modern, maintainable system.

**Recommendation:** Option 2 (Strangler Fig) with an immediate tactical decision on Oracle: do NOT renew the Oracle licence. Instead, migrate the database to PostgreSQL as a standalone project (£400K, 4 months) which removes the £1.2M annual cost immediately. This funds the modernisation from savings.

**Top 5 Risks:**
1. Oracle migration introduces data integrity issues — mitigate with parallel running and automated comparison
2. Mobile working capability takes longer than expected — mitigate by delivering it as an independent first slice
3. Caseworker resistance to new interfaces — mitigate with early user research and change management
4. Document management integration is more complex than estimated — mitigate with a discovery spike in month 1
5. Team cannot recruit modern technology skills fast enough — mitigate by using DOS7 framework for specialist contractors initially

**Next Steps:**
1. Do not renew Oracle licence (decision needed this month)
2. Commission Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration (4-month project)
3. Run discovery on mobile caseworker workflow (6 weeks)
4. Present Full Business Case at next board with detailed phase plan

reflectiveQuestions: Think about the oldest system in your department's estate. What makes it legacy — is it the age of the technology, the absence of skills, the architectural constraints, or the commercial arrangements? Would the CDDO framework classify it as high risk?
Have you been involved in a modernisation programme that failed or stalled? What went wrong — was it technical, political, commercial, or human? What would you do differently?
How would you approach knowledge extraction from a system with no documentation? What techniques would you use to verify that you have captured the full set of business rules?
When is retaining a legacy system the right decision? Can you think of a system in your organisation that should be left alone rather than modernised?
How do you balance the urgency of modernisation with the risk of disrupting critical services? Where would you draw the line between acceptable and unacceptable risk?

knowledgeCheck.question: According to the CDDO Legacy IT Risk Assessment Framework, what makes a system 'legacy'?
options: Any system older than 10 years
Any system not running on cloud infrastructure
A system that can no longer be changed safely, economically, or quickly enough to meet needs
Any system written in an older programming language like COBOL or Java
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Legacy is defined by the inability to change safely and economically, not by age or technology choice. The CDDO framework assesses Likelihood of negative outcomes and their Impact, focusing on factors like supportability, skills availability, security vulnerability, and ability to meet business needs.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the strangler fig pattern in legacy modernisation?
options: Completely replacing the legacy system in a single release
Gradually replacing components by routing traffic from legacy to new services slice by slice
Wrapping the legacy system in an API without changing it internally
Moving the legacy system to cloud infrastructure without changing its architecture
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The strangler fig pattern gradually replaces the legacy system by building modern replacements for individual slices of functionality and progressively routing traffic from the legacy system to the new components. Eventually the legacy system has no remaining traffic and can be decommissioned. It is named after the strangler fig tree that grows around its host.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most important factor when choosing between a rebuild and a strangler fig approach?
options: The age of the legacy technology
The risk tolerance of the organisation and the criticality of the system
The personal preference of the lead architect
Whether the system uses cloud or on-premise infrastructure
knowledgeCheck.explanation: For critical systems (processing payments, managing security, supporting essential services), the organisation's risk appetite typically pushes toward lower-risk incremental strategies like strangler fig. Rebuilds carry higher risk of disruption and are only appropriate when the legacy architecture is so fundamentally unsuitable that incremental improvement is not viable.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the strongest indicator that a strangler fig modernisation is succeeding?
options: The number of new microservices deployed
Feature delivery velocity improving as more functionality moves to the modern platform
The amount of money spent on the programme
The number of legacy components still running
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The purpose of modernisation is to make the system easier and faster to change. If feature delivery velocity is not improving as modernisation progresses, something is wrong — the modernisation may be addressing the wrong components or the new architecture may be introducing its own complexity. Velocity improvement is the outcome that justifies the investment.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary purpose of parallel running during legacy modernisation?
options: To double the system's processing capacity during the transition period
To verify that the new system produces the same correct outputs as the legacy system before routing live traffic
To give users a choice between the old and new interfaces
To reduce the cost of the legacy system by sharing its load
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Parallel running means operating both the legacy and new systems simultaneously, processing the same inputs, and comparing outputs to verify equivalence. This is essential for critical systems (especially those making financial calculations or eligibility decisions) where incorrect outputs have serious consequences. Only when parallel running demonstrates verified equivalence is live traffic routed to the new system.
